articles.title: Pope Leo is discharged from hospital, 4 days after undergoing lung cancer surgery
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV was released from Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Saturday, four days after undergoing surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his right lung . The pope exited via the hospital's main entrance. A large crowd waiting outside the hospital cheered for him. He shook hands with several people, then stopped to talk with a young woman who appeared to be wearing a bandage on her right arm and was holding a doll in the image of Pope Leo. The Pope was smiling. Once in the car, he waved to the crowd. His motorcade returned to Vatican City at 3:43 p.m. local time. The 71-year-old pope had a portion of his right lung removed and received a diagnosis of lung cancer earlier this week. No information about his prognosis has been publicly shared. Leo was initially expected to remain hospitalized until Oct. 20 but on Thursday he resumed some work activity , and doctors said Friday that tests confirmed "steady improvement in his recovery." On Saturday morning, the Vatican announced he would leave later in the afternoon. His personal physician and surgeon said in a separate statement that Leo was "deemed fit for discharge from the hospital" based on blood test results and a chest X-ray performed Saturday morning along with an assessment of his clinical condition. The Vatican also confirmed that Leo will recite the Angelus prayer from the window of the papal apartment on Sunday. The pontiff's surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, said in an interview with Vatican News that there is no clinical reason the Pope should skip an upcoming trip to South America. The visit, planned for early November, has been in question since Leo's hospitalization. On Friday, the Vatican published the names of journalists accredited to fly on the papal plane to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, signalling that the trip appeared to be going ahead. Leo also conducted some work from the hospital. The Vatican released pictures of the American-born pope standing at an altar in green vestments, celebrating Mass at a small chapel in Gemelli Hospital on Friday. The Vatican also said Leo spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin over the phone on Friday, during which he "expressed his deep concern about the grave humanitarian situation in the city of Oleshky" in Ukraine . The pope also held separate meetings with Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, the dean of the College of Cardinals, and Cardinal Baldassare Reina, the vicar general of the Diocese of Rome. In the interview with Vatican News, Margaritora said the discovery of the pope's lung tumor was "entirely accidental," and that he had no symptoms. The tumor was found at the base of the lung, Margaritora said, but if it had been "a little higher up, it certainly would not have been seen." "The Holy Father falls into the category of people who discover they have lung cancer entirely by chance – not because they are undergoing preventive screening, but because they undergo examinations for other reasons," Margaritora said. articles.title: Reported attacks on ships near Strait of Hormuz hit a new weekly high
articles.summary: What to know about the Iran war today: The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) monitoring agency said at least ten vessels have been attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz since last Sunday, a weekly high since war broke out in February, and 23 attacks were recorded since the start of the month, almost double the average.Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian denied Friday that Tehran sought nuclear weapons, expressed readiness for dialogue and condemned U.S. sanctions during talks with Georgia's prime minister.The Strait of Hormuz will reopen if the U.S. leaves the Middle East, a spokesman for Iran 's army said Friday. "If it does not leave, we will expel it," Mohammad Akraminia wrote on X . Saudi strikes on Yemen kill 12, Iran-backed Houthis say Saudi strikes that began overnight have killed at least 12 people in Yemen, three of them children, Houthi media reported on Saturday. Saudi warplanes targeted "civilian homes" in Taiz governorate on Saturday, killing nine people and wounding 16, the Iran-backed group's news agency said, adding people were still trapped under the rubble. The agency had earlier reported overnight strikes in Dhamar province that killed three children and wounded 17 other people. It said the strikes were carried out "using cluster bombs, which are banned internationally." The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis has launched daily raids in Yemen backing the internationally recognized government in the country's long-running civil war. Saudis intercept 4 drones over country in recent hours The Saudi-led coalition fighting against the Iran-backed Houthis have intercepted four drones over Saudi territory in the last few hours, the group said. The drones were intercepted over the capital city of Riyadh, and in the Eastern, and Southern regions, according to the coalition. The Houthis have regularly launched drones and missiles at the Saudis every day for the last several weeks. The coalition announced overnight it had taken out two missile-launch platforms in the Saada Governorate, which is the northern-most region in Yemen and controlled by the Houthis. A missile launch one week ago hit King Khallid International Airport in Riyadh and killed 13 people. President Sisi says Egypt ready to defend Saudi Arabia "if requested" Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Saturday said Egypt was ready to defend Saudi Arabia "if requested," as fighting flares between the kingdom and Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen. Since Yemen's war reignited in July, the Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi targets, including energy facilities and Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, where 13 people were killed in a single attack last Saturday. The Houthis have also blockaded the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Saudi-flagged tankers, piling pressure on energy exports as Iran presses its own blockade on the Strait of Hormuz. Speaking at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian military academy, Sisi said Egypt was "not looking for a role to play" in regional conflicts, but added it was "inconceivable" for Cairo to stand by while Saudi Arabia was "harmed or its security and stability threatened." "Egypt, of course, with the directives of His Majesty King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, will carry out any measure to protect you or defend you," he said. He added any deployment would require parliamentary approval and said he hoped lawmakers would convene in an emergency session to grant authorization "if it is requested of us." "I'm not talking about fighting anyone or attacking anyone," Sisi said. "We are speaking only about defense." Yemen's Houthis free 159 pro-government fighters under amnesty Yemen's Houthis on Saturday announced the release of 159 pro-government fighters under an amnesty announced after they seized swathes of land in a major offensive last month. The prisoners had "voluntarily surrendered themselves without fighting" as the Iran-backed group captured strategic positions along the Red Sea, Houthi official Abdelqader al-Murtada told a press conference in Sanaa. The Houthis' war with the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government reignited in July after four years of calm, triggering attacks on Saudi oil shipments and other targets including airports. The International Committee of the Red Cross confirmed the unilateral release of 159 prisoners and said it had given support by organizing interviews and health checks, contacting families and helping arrange transport. Murtada said 323 prisoners were released under the amnesty last month after surrendering in Hodeidah governorate. Iran backs "political process" to resolve Saudi-Houthi conflict, foreign minister says Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Saturday that Tehran supports a "political process" to resolve the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis. The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi targets, including energy facilities and Riyadh's international airport, where 13 people were killed in a major attack one week ago. "We support an inclusive and comprehensive political process as the only practical and sustainable way to resolve the issue," Araghchi said in a speech at the Organization of Islamic Cooperation in Baghdad. Araghchi repeated Iran's offer to mediate between the two sides. Deputy Foreign Minister Saeed Khatibzadeh previously said Riyadh has not responded to Iran's overture. On Friday, Iran denied having anything to do with the Houthi attacks, after Saudi Arabia accused Tehran of encouraging the group's escalation. In his speech, Araghchi also said "either we build security together, or we will endure insecurity together," adding Tehran was willing "to cooperate with all its brothers and neighbours to achieve the first option." The Houthis in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon are part of Iran's "Axis of Resistance" against Israel and the United States, which also includes armed groups in Iraq. Oil tanker reportedly hits mine in Strait of Hormuz Iran's Revolutionary Guards Corps on Saturday said an oil tanker was on fire in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a mine in the waterway at the heart of the Middle East war. "A supertanker in violation of regulations, carrying more than two million barrels of crude oil and attempting to pass illegally through the Strait of Hormuz, struck a mine, triggering an explosion and a fierce fire," the Iranian military said. The statement did not specify the exact location of the incident. "The tanker attempted to cross the strait with U.S. support... by deactivating all its tracking systems," the Guards added, also posting a video of a vessel in flames during the night. Ship attacked by RPG fired from small boat, British maritime agency said The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) monitoring agency reported on Saturday a second attack on a ship off the coast of Saudi Arabia, which took place a day early. In a post on social media , the UKMTO said: "The master of a tanker has reported being attacked by an RPG (rocket-propelled grenade) from a small boat, resulting in damage to the aft port quarter." Friday's attack is the second reported by the agency on that day off the coast of Al Jubayl in Saudi Arabia. "Crew are accounted for and reported safe," the UKMTO said, but the full extent of the damage and environmental impact were not known at the time of the report. Ship struck by "unknown projectile" off the coast of Saudi Arabia, maritime agency says A British maritime agency said Saturday it had received a report of a vessel struck on the Persian Gulf on Friday. The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said the tanker had been struck by an "unknown projectile" off the coast of Saudi Arabia. "All crew are reported safe and have been evacuated. There is no reported environmental impact at the time of report," the statement added. The UKMTO had previously reported that October had become the busiest month for reported attacks on ships in the Strait Hormuz. Reported shipping attacks jump in Strait of Hormuz, British monitor says A British monitor says October has become the busiest month for reported attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz since March, during the Iran war's opening months. That's as the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said it was "struggling to accurately report" the true number of attacks since most ships now refuse to report them. Still, UKMTO said 10 attacks were reported in the week ending Friday. One ship sank. Since early July, most attacks have occurred off Oman, where the U.S. military has been guiding vessels at risk of Iranian attack. There has been an uptick in attacks since President Trump late last month rejected a Tehran proposal to end the war and open the strait, though indirect negotiations have continued. 2 missiles strike airport in Yemen's port city of Aden, officials say Two missiles struck the airport in Yemen's port city of Aden on Friday night, police said, blaming Iran-backed Houthi rebels for the second such attack in less than a week. Police said no casualties were reported as fighting escalates in the latest front in the Iran war, one in which the rebels have attacked both neighboring Saudi Arabia and Yemen's internationally recognized government that's backed by the kingdom. A security official and a traffic controller told The Associated Press an area of the Aden airport that hosts a military unit aligned with the Saudi-backed government was hit. Both spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media. There was no immediate claim of responsibility. Iran denies Saudi accusation of involvement in Houthi attacks Iran's foreign ministry on Friday rejected Saudi Arabia's accusation that Tehran was involved in Houthi attacks on the kingdom, offering to mediate between the two sides. "The Islamic Republic of Iran rejects any claim that Iran has played a role in Yemeni (Houthi) operations," Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said in a statement, reiterating Tehran's offer to act as a bridge between the Houthis and Riyadh. Regardless of how involved Iran has been in Houthi attacks, the two groups have long held close ties . They were once a relatively marginal group within what Iran calls its Axis of Resistance — a loose alliance of anti-Israel, anti-U.S. militant groups that includes Hamas in Gaza and Hezbollah in Lebanon. "The Houthis are the most powerful proxy within the Iranian network, hands down," said Mohammed Al-Basha, founder of the Basha Report, a U.S.-based risk advisory group. "Any U.S. military strategy planning a campaign on Iran will have to take into consideration what the Houthis will do next." Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have killed about 20 people in the last several weeks, including 13 in one strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport last weekend. CBS/AFP Iran's president denies nuclear ambitions, says country ready for talks Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian denied Friday that Tehran sought nuclear weapons, expressed readiness for dialogue and condemned U.S. sanctions during talks with Georgia's prime minister. In his meeting with Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, Pezeshkian also called for closer ties with Georgia, weeks after Tbilisi cut aviation links between the two countries following U.S. sanctions targeting Iranian airlines. The two met on the sidelines of a U.N. biodiversity summit in Armenia's capital, Yerevan. "Iran is not seeking nuclear weapons, and we consider the malicious propaganda against our country to be lies," Pezeshkian said, according to a statement from his office. "We have always been ready for dialogue. They think they can force us to surrender, but we will not bow to coercion," he added, calling U.S. sanctions against Tehran "unjustifiable and inhumane." Georgia's Civil Aviation Agency said in September it would comply with U.S. sanctions, while Kobakhidze insisted Tbilisi was not imposing its own bilateral sanctions on Tehran. Saudi-hosted Asian Cup soccer tournament remains on schedule despite Houthi attacks Asian Cup organizers insisted Friday the continental soccer championship set to be held in Saudi Arabia in early 2027 remains on track despite a wave of missile and drone attacks on the host country in recent days. The Saudi organizing committee issued a statement Friday saying it is continuing to coordinate closely with the Asian Football Confederation. The tournament is scheduled for Jan. 7 to Feb. 5. "Preparations across all organizational and operational areas are progressing according to the approved schedule, including work on venues, facilities and supporting services," Saudi organizers said. "The focus remains on delivering a world-class tournament experience for participating teams, fans and media from across Asia, while bringing the continent together through football." South Korea's Professional Footballers' Association had earlier expressed concerns following a series of attacks on the Asian Cup host country by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels. "The continued military tensions and security instability in the Middle East are issues that can never be taken lightly," Lee Keun-ho, head of the South Korean player union, said in a statement. "The safety of our national team, as well as all players participating in the Asian Cup, is a serious concern." At least 19 people, including foreigners, have been killed in more than a week of Houthi attacks targeting the Riyadh international airport, the headquarters of Saudi oil giant Aramco and other aviation, oil and military facilities across the kingdom. Several sporting events have already been canceled or postponed in Saudi Arabia, including Netflix's Six Kings Slam tennis tournament; women's tennis' WTA Finals, which were moved to the U.S.; multiple matches for the Saudi soccer club Al-Nassr, which features Cristiano Ronaldo; and an Olympic qualifying event for BMX cycling. AP/CBS Attacks on Yemen government palace compound killed 5, officials say Attacks on the palace compound of Yemen's internationally recognized government Thursday killed at least five people and wounded more than a dozen others, government officials said. In a Facebook post late Thursday, Health Minister Qasem Buhaibeh said security guards and other employees at Maashiq palace in Yemen's southern port city of Aden were among the casualties. Aden has been the seat of Yemen's government since 2015. The Houthis claimed responsibility for the attacks, saying they targeted a military operations headquarters associated with Saudi forces backing the government. Two of the missiles launched by the Houthis on Thursday struck near the headquarters of the Saudi-backed coalition forces in Aden, causing damage, a Yemeni government official said. The official, speaking on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to speak to the media, said Friday the missiles landed near the compound used by the coalition in Buraiqah, a neighborhood west of the palace. No senior officials were there at the time of the attack, he said. Saudi-led coalition intercepts missiles and drones Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki announced a series of interceptions in successive X posts on Friday, saying Saudi forces had destroyed a ballistic missile, two cruise missiles and three drones over Saudi Arabia or the Red Sea. In a first tweet, Al-Maliki said coalition forces intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched toward Yanbu. A second post announced the interception and destruction of two cruise missiles over the Red Sea. He then reported three drones had been intercepted and destroyed in Saudi Arabia's southern region and the Riyadh region. Iraq says Iran war has deprived it of $60 billion in oil export revenue Iraq has lost around $60 billion during the U.S.-Iran war, Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said Thursday, as the fighting has blocked or severely impeded a waterway crucial to its oil exports. OPEC member Iraq was producing about 4 million barrels of oil per day (bpd) before the conflict, and exporting about 3.5 million bpd – mostly carried by tankers out of the Persian Gulf via the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's ongoing threat to vessels that fail to seek its permission to transit the strait has forced Iraq, which lacks sufficient storage capacity, to halt most production and fall back on limited exports via Syria and Turkey, by truck and pipeline respectively. Syria is set to provide an overland oil route to bypass the strait , the head of Syrian Petroleum Co. said last week. "Iraq has suffered losses estimated at around $60 billion during the recent war between the United States and the Islamic Republic of Iran," Hussein told his Italian counterpart in Rome, according to a statement from the Iraqi foreign ministry. After a heavy drop in production, Iraqi oil exports, which provide about 90% of the country's revenues, recovered modestly last month, reaching 2.6 million barrels per day between Sept. 1 and 21, according to the oil ministry. But at the same time, Iraq's foreign currency reserves have shrunk by $20 billion and consumer prices have risen sharply, plunging it into economic crisis. CBS/AFP Norwegian teen sentenced in U.K. to 20 years in prison for plotting murder for Iran-linked gang A Norwegian teenager convicted of traveling to Britain to carry out a contract killing on behalf of an international crime gang linked to Iran was sentenced Friday to 20 years in prison. Johannes Kongsnes Natland, 19, was found guilty in July of conspiracy to murder for agreeing to shoot someone unknown to him for $28,000 last year. He was arrested at a hotel in Huddersfield, in northern England, with two guns and ammunition two days after arriving in the U.K. In bodycam video released by police from the early hours of March 19, 2025, Natland emerges topless from his room and mimes a shooting gesture at a firearms officer before being slammed against a wall. It remains unknown who his intended target would have been. Natland, who was working part time at a pizza restaurant at the time of his arrest, was recruited by a Swedish organized crime group known as the Foxtrot Network while he was playing a game online. The group has links to the Iranian government, according to London's counterterrorism police unit. Natland was hired by a 17-year-old known as "Generalen." A court in Norway last year convicted the teenager of attempting to "contribute to murder" and sentenced him to 14 years in custody. A 16-year-old is awaiting trial in Norway for his role in the conspiracy. CBS/AP Iranian navy says a tanker is burning in the Gulf of Oman The Iranian navy said Friday that it had identified a tanker on fire in what it called a prohibited area in the Gulf of Oman, east of the Strait of Hormuz. The navy's public relations office said in a statement that military surveillance teams "discovered and identified a violating oil tanker that had caught fire in a prohibited area." The vessel had "switched off its tracking systems and was attempting to pass through a prohibited area in the Gulf of Oman." The navy did not say how the tanker "caught fire" but added that "the consequences of uncoordinated movements along routes and in prohibited areas are the creation of insecurity and serious hazards for other vessels." At least three commercial vessels have been struck in the region in suspected Iranian attacks this week. Iran says the Strait of Hormuz will reopen if the U.S. "leaves the region" The Strait of Hormuz will reopen if the U.S. "leaves" the Middle East, an Iranian army official said Friday. "If the United States leaves the region, the Strait of Hormuz will reopen and collective security will be established with the participation of the countries of the region, and the global economy will improve," army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia wrote on X . "If it does not leave, we will expel it." He did not elaborate on whether he was calling for a withdrawal of military forces sent during the current war, all U.S. military forces across the region, or military and non-military U.S. government personnel. Though there were credible reports earlier this month of oil exports from the Persian Gulf ramping back up to near pre-war levels , Iran and the U.S. continue offering conflicting narratives, with the Trump administration insisting the Strait of Hormuz is open, but Tehran claiming it is closed to all traffic unless Iranian authorities grant permission. Greek maritime risk firm Marisks warned Thursday that ships continue to face "indiscriminate attacks," even if they turn off their tracking systems, which many ships have been doing to avoid detection. Iran president says conflict in Mideast amounts to "ecocide" Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Friday urged countries to condemn what he called "ecocide" in the Middle East caused by "wars of aggression" against his country. Pezeshkian said the conflicts in Gaza and the wider Middle East had taken a significant toll on nature that extended beyond national borders and required "international solutions." "What has occurred in our region as a result of wars of aggression is ecocide, or environmental genocide, and it must be condemned," Pezeshkian said at a nature summit in Armenia that was attended by United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres. Pezeshkian decried an "atmosphere of distrust" between Iran and the U.S. in a recent interview with CBS News . "As long as they don't cease doing what they're imposing on us every day, it's difficult to trust them," he said. "Every day, they increase the sanctions against us. Every day, they threaten us. Every day, they strike us, and they don't honor what they have put in writing. So, if they engage in talks, will they actually follow through?" CBS/AFP White House prepares plans to use weapon dubbed "mother of all bombs" on Iran, sources say The White House and Pentagon have prepared plans to use a Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb to hit military sites in Iran if ordered by President Trump, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News. A Pentagon official told CBS News: "The Department of War plans for a wide range of operational scenarios to execute Presidential and Secretary level direction and to ensure mission success in any operational environment." A White House spokesperson said: "We do not comment on sensitive military plans that may or may not exist. President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon." Last week, Mr. Trump said the U.S. would not attack Iran before the midterm elections. He also touted "productive conversations" with Iran, though he did not provide specifics. CNN first reported Thursday on the plans to use the Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, or MOAB, on Iran. Mr. Trump set a precedent for using the MOAB, also known as the "mother of all bombs," when it was used in 2017 to attack an Islamic State cave complex in Afghanistan. The bomb is the largest U.S. non-nuclear weapon, weighing upwards of 30,000 pounds at a cost of $170,000 per unit. Read more here . articles.title: French police clash with protesters as tens of thousands rally over cost of living
articles.summary: By STAMOS PROUSALIS PARIS, Oct 17 (Reuters) - Clashes broke out between police and protesters in cities across France on Saturday as tens of thousands of people angered by  rising costs and declining public services took to the streets in some of the country's most violent protests in years. The Interior Ministry said ‌272 people had been arrested by mid-afternoon after violent incidents involving hooded individuals, including in Paris, Marseille in the south, Toulouse in the southwest, Angers ‌in the west and Lyon in east-central France. The protesters said most people were protesting peacefully and put much of the violence down to troublemakers who had set out to cause damage and clash with the police. The ​ministry said, however, that violence was increasing, and that there had been "confrontations with law enforcement, looting or attempted looting of shops, attacks on and damage to public buildings." It blamed the unrest on what it described as the "ultra-left". In some parts of Paris, police occasionally fired tear gas rounds as they retreated in the face of mostly young protesters, many of whom were dressed in black and wore hoodies, masks and  goggles to protect against tear gas. Some tourists at a fashionable department store near the Paris opera were seen spluttering when they were caught in ‌clouds of tear gas, and shops nearby were hastily shuttered. ⁠Windows of many shops and restaurants in the capital were smashed, and cars and trash cans were set on fire. In Lyon, protesters torched the tourist office. In Marseille, the mayor said the town hall had been vandalised and that additional police were being sent to the city ⁠following talks with the government. In protests partly inspired by those in France, several hundred mostly young people also protested in Brussels on Saturday, and some clashed with police. Belgian student groups have said they are protesting against rising education costs and reforms they fear will make higher education less accessible. Albania also faced more protests on Saturday, with police firing what appeared to be rubber ​bullets ​at protesters during a fifth day of mass student demonstrations calling for Prime Minister Edi Rama to ​step down. POLICE RESPONSE UNDER SCRUTINY The protests in France began last month ‌at high schools in Paris' poor northern suburbs, where anger over teacher shortages and shabby facilities evolved into a broader movement focused on inequality, public spending and living standards. "We are fighting because the cost of living is too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions," said Lola, a 19-year-old protester in Paris. A large police presence had been deployed in central Paris, especially near landmarks such as the Champs-Elysees and the Arc de Triomphe, which were excluded from the routes of two authorised demonstrations. Protesters in high-visibility vests blocked streets, ‌recalling the Yellow Vest movement that marked President Emmanuel Macron's previous term in office. Macron, who urged ​calm on Friday, is entering the final stretch of his presidency, facing a fragmented political landscape and growing ​pressure over the economy. France's efforts to reduce public debt have failed to reassure ​investors, pushing government borrowing costs to their highest levels in more than two decades. Police tactics have drawn criticism following a series of injuries ‌among demonstrators, including a teenager who lost a hand after picking ​up a stun grenade. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu ​said more than 900 police officers had also been injured in previous protests. The police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen allegations of police violence. France suspended the use of stun grenades during the student demonstrations, but Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said they could be used on Saturday. The Yellow Vest movement emerged in ​2018 in opposition to diesel taxes before expanding into a ‌wider protest against living costs and inequality. The movement subsided after Macron announced billions of euros in tax cuts. (Reporting by Clotaire Achi, Janis Laizans, Stamos ​Prousalis, Yann Tessier, Dominique Vidalon and Sybille de La Hamaide in Paris, Stephane Mahe in Nantes, Petra Wischgoll in Strasbourg, Marc Leras in Marseille. ​Writing by Sybille de La Hamaide. articles.title: Trump says neither he or Musk are to blame for Ukraine drone issues
articles.summary: Ukraine is still unable to use its interceptor systems against Russian drones, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday, because of speed restrictions imposed on Starshield, an upgraded military version of Elon Musk's Starlink, amid an ongoing row with President Trump. "Unfortunately, we can't use Starlink or Starshield technology on our territory today to shoot down jet-powered Shaheds," Zelenskyy said in an online group chat with reporters at the EU Summit. "They fly, and we can stop them with aircraft and other air defense, but we don't use Starlink for that, unfortunately. God willing, this will be restored." Zelenskyy said Kyiv was discussing the issue with U.S. officials, and he was told the restrictions were linked to technical issues. The Ukrainian president added, however, that Starlink appears to be operating at higher speeds on European Union territory. "Yes, we are in dialogue at the level of the military, the Ministry of Defense and diplomats, in touch with everyone including SpaceX. Nobody there is answering our military or the Ministry of Defense now," Zelenskyy said. "At various levels they say these are technical problems." "Here (in Ukraine) Starlink works up to a speed of 161 km/h, then shuts off," he continued. "In the EU it works at 180-plus and works constantly. Here it shuts off in the second minute after 161 km/h and stops working. We lose both drones and connectivity." Mr. Trump told reporters on Friday he had not limited Ukraine's access to Starlink, adding he didn't believe Musk, SpaceX's CEO, was responsible either. "Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Mr. Trump said while leaving the White House to travel for a rally in Georgia. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been." Musk said Wednesday he isn't responsible for deciding how Starshield is used, writing on X: "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS." Starshield is essential to Ukraine's armed forces as it allows personnel to communicate and carry out strikes, including by maintaining contact with drones across long distances. On Saturday, Zelenskyy said Russia carried out a large attack on Ukraine's energy sector, targeting more than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities across the country. A day earlier, the president said the current restrictions on Starshield had left people vulnerable to Russian drones, which was "very painful and frustrating" Ukrainian officials and soldiers told CBS News the country's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment late Tuesday, including speed limits that made it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones. Sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions. Mr. Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with Zelenskyy in recent days, blaming the war between Russia and Ukraine for high global energy prices. The Trump administration waived restrictions on buying Russian diesel last week in an effort to ease pressure, a move Zelenskyy argued could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin. In a social media post on Saturday, Zelenskyy called the move "unfortunate," adding the act, championed by late Sen. Lindsey Graham, "could have helped enormously." Later, he told journalists he believed the Trump administration will lift more sanctions on Russia. "Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue. I believe the 'diesel deal' is just the first step," Zelenskyy told reporters. CBS News has reached out to the White House for comment. Mr. Trump said Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure — announcing an "energy ceasefire" over the weekend. Zelenskyy initially said Ukraine was willing to abide by such an agreement, but that Russia's strikes never ceased, and several days later he told the Financial Times his country would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries because Russia was still attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. The Russian government never confirmed it had agreed to a ceasefire. In a Newsmax interview late Thursday, Mr. Trump called Zelenskyy "not a good guy for us to deal with," argued Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries would be a "disgrace," urged both sides to make a deal and said the Ukrainian leader is harder to deal with than Putin. "I'm not a big fan of Zelenskyy," Mr. Trump said. On Wednesday, Musk had tweeted : "Time for Zelensky to go." articles.title: Judge denies gag order request in Cornell sex assault civil case
articles.summary: A New York judge on Friday rejected a request to impose a gag order in the civil case brought by a former Cornell University student who alleged she was sexually assaulted at a fraternity house in 2024, calling the request a "'side show' meant to muddy the waters and distract from the merits of the claims and defenses involved in this case." Judge Phaedra Perry-Bond said the public statements made by Jane Doe's attorney that one of the men named in the civil lawsuit used to justify the request "express nothing more than [his] opinions." Cornell president defends response to Jane Doe allegations in heated faculty meeting "Expressing opinions on the case or reporting on how the litigation has impacted clients cannot alone serve as a factual basis for limiting an individual's First Amendment rights," Judge Perry-Bond wrote. "While the Court agrees that [he] should not make statements that certain parties spoliated evidence, especially where, as here, no discovery has yet to take place, those isolated statements, without more, are insufficient to show the serious risk of prejudice required by precedent and the United States Constitution." The judge encouraged the attorneys in the case to work together to prevent their clients from facing threats, harassment, and doxing. "The Court believes that given the notoriety of doxing related to this case, it would serve all parties' interests to work together to ensure their clients and others may be safeguarded, to the extent possible, from being inundated with threats or harassment from malicious outside actors," she wrote. Angelina Katsanis/Reuters - PHOTO: Cornell University in Ithaca, New York Perry-Bond also rebuked the lawyer who requested the gag order for including in a court filing an email exchange with an attorney for one of the other men. "The Court will not tolerate its docket being used to generate media controversy, and this Court does not tolerate attorneys, especially attorneys who are not even involved in this case, engaging in mudslinging," she wrote. The attorneys requesting the gag order had asked for "narrowly tailored restrictions" that would prevent lawyers and parties in the civil case from commenting on the allegations outside of court, arguing in their motion that a gag order would limit "possible juror prejudice" and prevent the potential release of sensitive information that could lead to " threats, doxing, intimidation, and extrajudicial contact." In a statement responding to the motion response, an attorney for Jane Doe, Thomas Giuffra, argued that the attorney for one of the men "has tried to rebut the claims in this case by engaging in a wholesale leaking of confidential documents, giving interviews calling Ms. Doe's story into question and calling her lawsuit immoral. These attempts to shift the narrative have not been successful." Accused Cornell University student asks for gag order A then-undergraduate student identified only as Jane Doe made a complaint to campus police in November 2024, three weeks after the alleged incident occurred, that she had been sexually assaulted by a group of men at the Chi Phi fraternity house. She filed a civil suit against seven men and the university alleging that she had been drugged and raped. The men denied all of the allegations. The university has said it takes allegations of allegations of sexual violence "extremely seriously" and that it "investigated and adjudicated the allegations consistent with university policies." The school said it conducted a "thorough" Title IX investigation and "issued a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell. This week, Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff announced that all parties and social events at fraternity houses are suspended for the rest of year while the university considers whether fraternity life can continue at the Ivy League school. "It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action," Kotlikoff said Tuesday. No criminal charges have been filed, but an investigation by the New York attorney general is ongoing. The case has rocked the university and started conversations about treatment of sexual assault allegations on college campuses across the country. articles.title: Trump is hitting the campaign trail. But he's largely missing from GOP ads.
articles.summary: Donald Trump is barnstorming the country to boost Republicans in the final weeks of the midterms. But many candidates want to keep that support quiet. The president is nowhere to be found in GOP ads, even in red states where Republicans were happy to tout his endorsement two years ago. And some candidates are hesitant to appear with Trump on the campaign trail — even as they hope he will help juice turnout among the MAGA base in November. Democratic House and Senate candidates and outside groups have spent $145 million on general election ads mentioning Trump, while Republicans have spent just $8 million, according to a POLITICO analysis of data from AdImpact, which tracks political advertising. That's in sharp contrast to 2024, when GOP candidates spent $62 million on ads mentioning Trump. "Trump is at historic lows right now, so if he comes to your district or state, it's about getting the Republican base vote out there and that can certainly help," said Ron Bonjean, a longtime GOP strategist. "But it's really important for the candidates not to be talking about Trump 24/7 on the campaign trail." The unfavorable national political environment leaves few incentives for GOP candidates to tie themselves to Trump, and more and more Republicans in competitive races have broken with the president on issues such as the Iran war and tariffs. When Republicans do mention Trump in ads, they often aren't touting his support. In Alaska, GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan has run an ad citing how he "voted to force Trump's DOJ to release the Epstein files." The silence on the airwaves is especially stark in red states like Nebraska and Ohio. In 2024, Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Neb.), who was facing a challenge from independent Dan Osborn, and now-Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), who was challenging then-Sen. Sherrod Brown, both ran several general election ads featuring endorsements from Trump. The president won Nebraska by more than 20 points and Ohio by 12 points that year, with Fischer and Moreno also winning their races. But this cycle, the GOP isn't focusing its ads on Trump in either state, as the match-up between Osborn and Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts heats up in Nebraska and Brown seeks to oust Republican Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio. Both Ricketts and Husted appeared at Trump rallies earlier this month. Still, Trump is absent from all Republican Senate ads in Ohio, and the only Ricketts ads that name the president accuse Osborn of disparaging Trump supporters — but don't mention Trump's endorsement. "The war in Iran, I think, has become a real noose around the neck of Republican candidates because of the affordability crisis," said former Ohio Rep. Jim Renacci. A nonprofit he works with surveyed voters on whether GOP candidates should appear with Trump and found that "in most cases you do not want [Trump] standing near you, which is why I was a little bit surprised that Jon Husted has had two events with President Trump, because I do believe there's a strong headwind in Ohio, and a big change from 2024." Husted's campaign spokesperson Amy Natoce told POLITICO in a statement, "President Trump won Ohio decisively three times by 8 points, 8 points and 11 points. If we successfully turn out the MAGA vote this November, then we will retire Sherrod Brown for good." The National Republican Senatorial Committee did not respond to a request for comment. "President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress," White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said. "The choice has never been more clear: doubling down on President Trump's winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats' extreme liberal policies and obstruction." Another Republican operative, who is based in Ohio and like others was granted anonymity to speak candidly about their own party, said GOP candidates need to find a way to talk about the Trump administration — no tax on tips, protecting social security — without mentioning the guy in the Oval Office. "This is a historically unpopular president," said the strategist, who has worked on multiple statewide races over the course of the last 15 years. "We all agree with that, and so it's kind of hard to attach yourself on the airways, I think, too closely to him." Trump's rallies, unlike candidates' ads, are seen more as targeting the president's base. He's not only visiting traditional battlegrounds like Georgia and Michigan, but also typically safe red states like Alabama and Kansas. Still, his events have been a source of tension with some GOP candidates. When Trump's team was making plans for the president to campaign in Michigan last week potentially in western Michigan, several Republican candidates and their teams up and down the ticket initially didn't know whether they should attend and be seen with the president, according to three Republicans with direct knowledge of the conversations, who were granted anonymity to share private details. They were concerned about being associated with Trump's tariffs, which have hammered the state, along with high fuel prices amid the Iran war. Trump officials scrapped the event and said the president would visit the state later in the month. Trump is now scheduled for a rally in the state on Oct. 25. "[Republican candidates] are going to do what they need to do," said one GOP pollster close to the White House. "What the White House and the president are doing is they are targeting places where they think the president can be helpful." Trump has allowed Republicans to discuss issues pertaining to their states or districts as "he understands that it is not a balk on him," said one White House official, granted anonymity to speak candidly. If Trump "was to believe that all these individuals were balking him, I A) don't think that he would want to be on the road every day, and B) I do think that you would probably see a more vocal President Donald J. Trump on Truth, et cetera, kind of voicing his opinion on it," the official said. The president and his team are giving most Senate GOP candidates especially a wide latitude to break with some of his policies at times, according to two other White House officials involved in the conversations. Trump, they said, understands the need for vulnerable candidates to create some distance, even though in the past he has lashed out at members of his party for similar moves. Republicans in the more MAGA-friendly House, however, are expected to run more in lock-step with the president. Only the most at-risk candidates are afforded some room to break with Trump, the officials said, given the tidal wave of chaos that can spur within the conference. One GOP strategist working on a battleground House race, granted anonymity to discuss private information, said he had gotten pre-approved from the White House for his candidate to miss a planned rally. Still, the strategist cautioned, that doesn't mean Trump won't berate someone from the stage when he notices the candidate is missing. Republicans still see Trump as a unique motivator for his base and rallies as a tool to help turn out voters who might be driven by the president. With Democratic voters already energized by opposing Trump, the GOP has less to lose by bringing the president out to turn out MAGA voters too. "The reality is, Democrats are going to vote in this midterm," said Paul Shumaker, a Republican strategist from North Carolina, where Trump is set to return for a rally next week as GOP Senate nominee Michael Whatley struggles to close the gap in his race. "And what Republicans need to be doing is focus on what they can do to improve their voter turnout on their side." Lauren Fedor, Myah Ward, Andrew Howard and Alex Gangitano contributed to this report. articles.title: An armed dad and a teacher stopped an Oregon school shooter. It took just 3 minutes.
articles.summary: Community members grieve at the site of a makeshift memorial in front of Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, on October 16. - Mathieu Lewis-Rolland/Getty Images On a sunny Oregon fall morning, parents dressed their children up and sent them to Silver Rail Elementary School for picture day. It’s the kind of picture parents return to years later, marveling at how small their children once were and how their smiles looked before their faces changed. But for some families, snapshots in their minds from that morning will carry a devastating, final memory of a child who never came home. Just hours after Steven and Angela Nuchols sent their 8-year-old daughter to school, they raced back to Silver Rail, desperate to know whether she was alive, they told local news outlet , The Bend Source . “It was crawling with police officers from all over the county,” Angela Nuchols told The Bend Source . “You’ve got guys in tactical gear, rifles. You’re just scared to death wondering, is your child OK?” For the Nuchols family, the next few hours before they were reunited with their daughter at a church were “the worst three hours of our lives,” Angela said. unknown content item - American schools have repeatedly seen the illusion of safety shattered within the walls of their classrooms. An elementary school in Bend, Oregon, was the latest among them, when a 16-year-old opened fire on Thursday, killing three children, including Rhoam Summer, aged 5; and two others, aged 8 and 11; as well as a 25-year-old teacher, Megan Lambert, police said. A 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were injured and taken to local hospitals, according to officials. When Gretchen Miller learned there was an active shooter at Silver Rail Elementary School, she called her husband and sprinted the block from their home to the school, where their son was inside. Ring camera video captured Miller racing down the street, frantically screaming, “There’s an active shooter at Silver Rail. Oh my God, oh my God, oh my God.” Another school turned into a crime scene; a violation of the sanctity of childhood. A drone view shows Silver Rail Elementary School, the day after a shooting, in Bend, Oregon, October 16. - David Ryder/Reuters 180 seconds of terror Michelle was a freshman in high school in California when she survived a school shooting in 2001. The trauma followed her into adulthood; she learned to scan rooms for exits, sit facing doors and live with anxiety and panic attacks. Long before the shooting, every school drop-off carried a quiet dread. Michelle, who is withholding her last name for privacy, would watch her children go, a pit in her stomach, wondering whether she would see them again. Then, on Thursday, her fifth-grade son called from Silver Rail Elementary School. “Mom, there’s a shooter.” Michelle was eating at an Olive Garden when her son’s voice came through his Apple Watch. She cried while recounting the moment, and said she immediately knew from the sound of his voice that something was terribly wrong. She told him she loved him, urged him to stay quiet and hung up to call 911. As she ran to her car, the call rang without an answer. She raced toward the school, about 10 minutes away. “I was like, how can this happen?” Michelle wonders, her voice shaking. “How can lightning strike twice?” A mother who lived through a 2001 school shooting comforts her son during Silver Rail Elementary shooting. - Michelle The first 911 call came at 12:59 p.m., after the driver of a red pickup truck saw a man approach the school, throw his long gun over the fence and climb over after it, police said Friday. When the pickup driver confronted him, the suspect opened fire, striking the truck at least three times. From her classroom window, fifth-grade teacher Kathy Sheil Smith watched the gunman walk toward the building. She called the main office, then pulled her students into a corner. “They were so afraid. The looks on their faces, it was really hard to see,” Sheil Smith told CNN affiliate KPTV, trying to hold back tears. “Some kids were praying, some kids were consoling other kids. But they were doing so quietly because they know you don’t make any noise.” She wondered whether she would live to see the end of the day. What mattered to her was that her students would. “I’m sure that every teacher at the school thought, ‘Today is the day that I am going to die,’” Sheil Smith told CNN affiliate KPTV . “Save my kids.” As Smith tried to shield her students inside the school, a terrifying picture was emerging. Around 12:59 p.m., emergency dispatchers received a flood of calls reporting that a person had entered the Silver Rail Elementary School and started shooting, according to Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz. At 1:01 p.m., police directed the school to go into lockdown. “Ms. Hawkins, the principal, was saying ‘lockdown, lockdown,’ and then the shots kept on going and going,” one 9-year-old student told CNN affiliate KGW , describing how he hid under a sink for 30 minutes, fearing the gunman would approach his classroom next. “I’m pretty sure a girl. She was saying, ‘Please, please, no,’ and then it was a shot and then dead silence,” he added. The gunman went directly into the classroom just left of the entrance and fired as many as 15 rounds, according to Krantz. The classroom was dedicated to special needs students, according to Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook. A second driver, a 36-year-old father whose children attend the school, had witnessed the initial shooting, drove into the school parking lot and followed the suspect into the school with his legally secured 40-caliber pistol, police said. The bystander was identified by his family as Kaylub Giamanco on Friday. A drone view shows a vehicle belonging to Kaylub Giamanco, the bystander who fatally shot the suspect, in a cordoned-off area at Silver Rail Elementary School, the day after a shooting, in Bend, Oregon, October 16. - David Ryder/Reuters A teacher — who was not injured — threw her cellphone at the shooter and tackled him in an attempt to get the gun away from him, the police chief said. When Giamanco heard gunfire and saw the teacher physically struggling with the gunman, Giamanco entered the classroom and fired, striking the suspect multiple times and killing him, police said. Less than half a mile away, business owner Sierra Jordan told CNN the familiar sound of children laughing and playing outside at recess gave way to the frantic arrival of ambulances. About three minutes after the first 911 call, it was over: At 1:02 p.m., police arrived and reported the shooter had been shot and killed by Giamanco. President Donald Trump called Giamanco “a great hero” who “took care of business.” A photo of Kaylub Giamanco - Kaylub Giamanco/Facebook “Had this not happened, had the bystander not neutralized the shooter? This could have been a much more tragic event than it was,” former FBI special agent Ken Gray told CNN. The shooter was identified as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, a former special needs student at the school, Krantz said Friday. A Maverick 88 pump-action, 12-gauge shotgun was found near the suspect, who had about 44 remaining rounds of 12-gauge ammunition, Krantz added. The gun had been purchased by his mother, a senior law enforcement official briefed on the investigation told CNN earlier Friday. Tragedy plunges community into grief Bend, a picturesque city of about 100,000 people, sits in the high desert landscape of central Oregon. It is a city of sage-scented air, snow-capped peaks and the Deschutes River that cuts through the heart of downtown; a magnet for thrill-seekers finding solace in the nearby mountain trails, red rock cliffs and star-filled skies. Although the city has boomed in recent years, it remains a quiet corner of the American West where the wilderness begins just beyond the city streets and its brick front stores and breweries. “Bend is a place that people move to from bigger cities,” Former Bend Mayor Jeff Eager told CNN . “They move here because it’s relatively safe here; they move here because we have schools you can walk your kids to,” Eager said. “You can’t imagine that it happens here.” But against Bend’s picturesque backdrop, the aftermath looked devastatingly familiar. Parents rushing to a reunification center, hearts clenched with the hope of finding their children among the survivors. Police tape cordoned off the school as officers stood guard. An emergency worker holds up police tape at the scene of a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, October 15. - Rob Kerr/Reuters The minutes had passed so quickly for the rest of the world, but for the families waiting to learn whether their children were alive, the abrupt end of the gunfire wasn’t the end of their agony. The prevalence of school shootings in America should prompt a conversation about “responsible gun ownership,” Democratic Rep. Janelle Bynum of Oregon told CNN. “This school, we had invested money in to make sure that it was locked. They did all of their drills as expected — everything that we’ve said that will protect kids up to now, and yet it didn’t work,” she said. “The laws don’t go far enough, fast enough for us to be able to intervene,” Bynum said. “We have to stop allowing our children to be shredded in schools, grocery stores, parks, churches. We have to stop this violence.” Investigators seek answers The Bend-La Pine school district — of which Silver Rail Elementary School is part — has multiple security measures in place such as secure entry vestibules, photo ID checks and visitor screenings, indoor and outdoor security cameras and upgraded locks on classroom doors that can be secured from inside, according to the district. Despite those measures, some of which were upgraded in 2022, the gunman was able to force his way into the elementary school by shooting at locked doors. It is not yet clear why the shooter was able to bypass security measures, the district’s superintendent said. Investigators are still working to establish a motive for the shooting, authorities said Friday. A search warrant was executed at the alleged shooter’s house on Thursday, according to a senior law enforcement official, who told CNN c omputers and other electronics were taken. Search warrants have also been obtained to gain access to the devices and extract data, according to the source. Local law enforcement and the FBI will examine the material for evidence that could help explain what led to the shooting. The shooter’s parents were cooperative and told investigators their son had attended Silver Rail Elementary School during their interview, the source said. During the pandemic, the shooter’s mother spoke with CNN affiliate KTVZ about her hopes that in-person classes would resume for children with special needs. The program was described as serving children with “intensive behavioral and social skills challenges.” She spoke briefly with CNN off camera from her balcony on Friday but declined to comment on how her son got access to the weapon. Authorities say that is still under investigation. The woman told CNN there were no warning signs. “I miss my boy. I’m so sorry,” the woman said as she cried and smoked a cigarette. In a message to the families of those killed, she said: “I’m so sorry, I wish I could have done something. I’m sorry for their loss.” Another chorus of thoughts and prayers Members of the Bend community gathered downtown in Drake Park on Thursday evening for a prayer vigil to support each other and grieve. Bend Mayor Melanie Kebler spoke while in tears alongside Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek, who was also crying. A large crowd of mourners held candles and hugged one another as they listened to prayers, music and community leaders. People wrote tributes in chalk. “NEVER again,” one person wrote. “Be at peace,” scribbled another. A young child knelt to place a lit candle on a step. By Friday, a makeshift memorial had taken shape outside Silver Rail Elementary School. Bouquets of flowers, toys and red, heart-shaped balloons lined a nearby crosswalk, just beyond yellow police tape. One mother, Ally Land, brought her children, 8 and 5, to the memorial. Her children don’t attend Silver Rail, but Land said she wanted to help them understand what had happened, answering their questions as best she could. “I asked them what they knew, and they just said, ‘I know that school’s canceled, so that they can make school safer tomorrow,’” Land told CNN . “We told them something terrible had happened, and we just followed their questions from there.” All Bend-La Pine Schools were closed on Friday, including activities and athletic events, the district said. But a day without classes cannot prevent the next shooting. The Silver Rail Elementary tragedy is the 36th shooting in the United States this year on K-12 school grounds, according to CNN’s analysis of multiple databases, including the Gun Violence Archive. “As a country, we still lack the courage to do anything to try to prevent these things from occurring,” CNN’s Senior Law Enforcement Analyst Charles Ramsey told CNN’s Elex Michaelson on Friday. “And it’s going to happen again.” Blake and Danielle Brinker were at their home outside Bend with Blake’s mother when they learned of the shooting, they told CNN. Blake said, describing his emotions at the time, as “just absolutely gutted.” The pair, who know people directly affected by the shooting, also visited the memorial. “Immediately could feel the energy of the community just stop on a dime,” Blake said. Danielle described Bend as “a very magical place.” A woman lights a candle during a candlelight vigil at Drake Park for victims of the Silver Rail Elementary School shooting, in Bend, Oregon, October 15. - David Ryder/Reuters The town was named in the top 75 safest midsize cities in the country, according to a SmartAsset study earlier this year. But Thursday’s deadly shooting isn’t the first in Bend. In 2022, a 20-year-old gunman, a Bend resident, killed two people after walking into a grocery store with an AR-15-style rifle and opening fire. Back in Bend, Cook, the district superintendent at Bend-La Pine Schools, spent Friday with staff at the school who are grappling with the devastating aftermath. “They are in so much pain, as we all are,” Cook said. “This has been a terrifying and traumatic experience that will affect us all profoundly for years to come.” Michelle, the 2001 school shooting survivor and a mother of children at Silver Rail Elementary School, carried for years the knowledge that gun violence could shatter an ordinary day without warning. But she’d hoped her children would never have to know what that’s like. “My friend said to me, this is generational trauma, this is a second generation that’s been through school shooting trauma,” Michelle told CNN. “How sick is that?” CNN’s Taylor Galgano, Helen Regan, Emma Tucker, Norma Galeana, Caroll Alvarado, Alisha Ebrahimji, Amanda Jackson, Leigh Waldman, John Miller, Rebekah Riess, Elise Hammond and Yan Kaner contributed to this report. articles.title: Online forum controlled by Nevada GOP House candidate contains slurs and Nazi talk
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — Long before running for Congress , Marty O’Donnell was an award-winning music composer for the popular “Halo” video game franchise. His work drew legions of fans to an online forum, which the Nevada Republican has tried to turn into a galvanizing force as he tries to unseat a Democrat in a Las Vegas area district that could help decide House control . O’Donnell has served as the group’s de facto leader, referring to himself as its “benevolent dictator” while tapping its members for campaign cash and harnessing their enthusiasm in his bid. The campaign held a two-day event for forum members this month at a casino that included a video game tournament, panel discussions and speeches. There is another side, however, to what is known as “The Marty Army.” An Associated Press review of thousands of posts made on the forum between 2022 and 2026 found racial slurs, minimizations of Nazi Germany and defenses of white nationalist conspiracy theories. “It wasn’t a couple of crazies. The popular sentiment was, ‘Yes, slavery should be legal,’” said Deacon Dameron, a former group member who said O’Donnell banned him for calling another user a “dork.” Many views espoused in the forum, which is controlled by O’Donnell and his handpicked moderators, are at odds with some of the values articulated by the candidate and his campaign. For example, O’Donnell has staunchly defended Israel and condemned bigotry. In a statement, campaign spokesman Keith Schipper said O’Donnell “has zero tolerance for hate" in his forum. Since becoming aware of the issue in the spring, the campaign “dedicated a staffer to monitor” and “remove people that spew racist and antisemitic vitriol,” Schipper said. “Unfortunately, some posts have been missed over the years.” Schipper said nearly 200 users have been banned “because of hateful rhetoric, including many of the people flagged by the Associated Press. Marty’s support of Israel is unequivocal and, as seen in various interviews and online posts, he will not tolerate the rise of antisemitism in our country. Marty will continue to fight bigotry, misinformation, and hate toward Israel because it is the right and moral thing to do.” O’Donnell, who is endorsed by President Donald Trump, is running against four-term Rep. Susie Lee in the Nov. 3 election as Republicans look to hang onto their razor-thin majority. In a sign of how Republicans are triaging their chances in a tough environment, they pulled back spending this week in a handful of congressional races, including O’Donnell’s. From ‘Halo’ to emoji slurs Most of the chat group’s comments concern video games and gaming strategies. A section is reserved for questions about O’Donnell’s work on “Halo” games. After O’Donnell announced his first run for Congress in 2024, when he finished fourth in the party primary, some discussions centered around news and policy. Many of the offensive and controversial remarks came in freewheeling replies to otherwise anodyne comments about current events, politics or games. In May 2022, for example, a member wrote, “WE STAND WITH MARTY.” Others reacted to the post using letter emoji to spell out — incorrectly — a racial slur for Black people. More soon chimed in, using emoji letters to invoke another anti-Black slur. Users were likely restricted from properly spelling out such words because, by design, the platform prevents emoji from being used more than once in reaction to a post. During a January 2025 discussion concerning free speech, a forum member expressed a desire to use a racial slur but refrained because “that’s not the attention Marty wants.” Dameron, the former group member, and another former user said posters relied on coded language because more overt racist comments were likely to draw scrutiny from moderators. The other user spoke on condition of anonymity over fears of retaliation. “The Marty Army” began as a fan forum “The Marty Army” began as an inside joke. Developers of “Halo” created the chat room in 2001 on a website devoted to the game. The name they chose was meant to invoke a club for rabid fans of the glam rock band Kiss. O’Donnell joined the chat group and assumed control of the forum. He relocated it to Discord, a popular online platform. His candidate website contains a link to the Discord chat group, which he has also publicized from his account on the social media platform X. “Hey all! If you’d like to be part of my run for Congress, you can be part of Marty’s Army,” O’Donnell said in an X post after he launched his 2024 campaign. O’Donnell has stated repeatedly that users who espouse racist or antisemitic views will be banned. He also threatened, at times, to delete posts. The AP found some users who espoused Nazi sympathies were kicked off the forum, but many of their posts remain. A user suggested in March 2024 that the Nazis “did some good things” that were “completely overshadowed by the terrible things they did.” Another that month asked, “Was Hitler really an evil guy?” “Like aside from the Holocaust,” the user added, “did he really even do anything wrong?” In February, a third member posted, “Heil Hitler.” O'Donnell said he wore a Mussolini mask Current and historical fascist figures have also drawn approval. O’Donnell wrote on the forum that he rejects fascism. But he also shared a photo of himself wearing what he said was a mask of Benito Mussolini, the Italian dictator and key Hitler ally, that he wore to a Halloween party. O'Donnell's campaign denied he dressed up as Mussolini. “This mask was part of a scary Halloween costume nearly two decades ago. It was not labeled a Mussolini mask when he bought it nor was he dressed up as Mussolini for the holiday,” Schipper said. “He purchased it because it was the ugliest, creepy mask on the shelf. He jokingly referred to it as a ‘Mussolini mask’ years later because he realized it vaguely looked like Mussolini.” O’Donnell stated this year that he had been unaware of the resurgence of antisemitism. He told a conservative news outlet in September that he thought “that antisemitism is something we don’t have to worry about anymore.” “I guess it just went under the surface and it has been percolating there,” he added in the interview with the Washington Reporter, which was founded by Republican political strategists. O’Donnell made the comment after the news site Jewish Insider reported that he hosted Charles Cornish-Dale, a far-right influencer with Nazi sympathies, on his own podcast, “The Marty O’Donnell Show.” O’Donnell pledged to ban those who espouse antisemitism In the spring, O’Donnell warned users on the forum that if there was “even a hint of antisemitism” the offending member would be “instantly banned.” Users responded to his post with an emoji of an exaggerated nose and “GOY,” a sometimes disparaging Yiddish term for non-Jews. Some anti-hate groups view the use of the nose emoji as antisemitic, while goy is a term that has been appropriated by those who espouse antisemitic views. Wendy Melillo, an associate professor of journalism at American University who researches extremist chat rooms, said such comments were clearly “coded antisemitic hate speech.” Melillo said other posts she reviewed were more explicit. “There is nothing coded,” she said, “about ‘Heil Hitler.’” Some members of “The Marty Army” are aware the forum could pose a liability. In 2024, a user wrote that O’Donnell’s political career could face trouble “if someone does a vulnerability study and they find this server.” This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/online-forum-controlled-nevada-gop-123530042.html

articles.title: Proposed bill could be the break Hollywood has been waiting for
articles.summary: The beleaguered U.S. film and TV industry, which has seen significant dollars leave for foreign countries, local production plummet and thousands of jobs vanish, may have some relief on the way. It comes in the form of proposed legislation that has the rare support of lawmakers across the political spectrum. Indeed, President Donald Trump and the actors union SAG-AFTRA have been equally vocal in throwing their weight behind the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act, which aims to create a significant tax incentive to bring Hollywood back home. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. The bill was introduced in Congress in late September and is now with the House Ways and Means Committee. Given the bipartisan support, it is likely to have a relative glide path on Capitol Hill. “Both parties represent people who work on sets, run catering companies and own hotels,” said Rep. Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas), who co-wrote the bill. “Co-sponsors come from California, Georgia, New York, Ohio and Tennessee, and every one of us has heard the same thing at home: The work is going overseas.” For film and TV creatives and craftspeople, the bill can’t land on the White House’s Resolute Desk a moment too soon. “Whatever you think about the current administration, at least Trump, if he puts his weight behind this, could actually make this really move quickly, which is what we need,” said Carolina Groppa, an Emmy-nominated producer who also hosts a podcast, “Angle on Producers,” about the industry. “The patient’s been on the gurney for a long time, collectively across the United States.” Film and TV production has indeed been fleeing Los Angeles for years - and often leaving the U.S. entirely. Other countries, from Ireland and Canada to Serbia and Colombia, have introduced huge tax incentives that have enticed producers to move projects to wherever is best for the bottom line. According to a recent report from EY Quantitative Economics and Statistics, the share of production spending for studio films with primarily U.S.-based projects declined since the turn of the century from 74 percent to 42 percent; for TV, it fell from 94 percent to 64 percent. That trend accelerated following the 2023 SAG-AFTRA and Writers Guild of America strikes, which were themselves triggered in part by industry contraction following the pandemic. “You could just feel the town change,” said Elsbeth Mumm, a set decorator based in Los Angeles. “Shows were being canceled, movies were getting pushed, scripts were just disappearing, things that had gotten green-lit were just stopped.” The people who have been hurt most are the middle class of the entertainment industry: the writers, production staff and craftspeople who often live project to project. When filmmaking fled overseas, many of their lives changed. “People are losing houses,” Mumm said. “People have lost their health care. People have lost their retirement.” The federal program would give certain film and TV productions a 20 percent tax rebate. To qualify, they would have to cost over $1 million, with at least 75 percent of the principal photography days occurring domestically. The bill would allow the federal rebate to be stacked on top of existing state incentives. “If what is in the bill goes through and is executed as promised, it will be a massive game changer,” said Patrick Meaney, an independent film director. “I think people are almost underrating it or not really processing it because it came out of nowhere and seems too good to be true.” The tax incentive structure is somewhat similar to a smaller plan in effect in California, which last year was significantly broadened to include up to $750 million in credits annually. Many in Hollywood feel the program’s expansion has been a success. The outlook is hopeful “for the first time in a long time,” said Keith Raskin, a veteran producer currently working on a crime comedy, “Sunset P.I.,” which is set to premiere on NBC in 2027. He’s filming in Los Angeles thanks to the state tax rebate program. “When I make phone calls to crew members to hire them, they cry because it means that they can make a payment on their house or they can keep their insurance for another year.” If the federal rebate passes, it would mean “we’re finally a player in the world market,” Raskin added. One big difference from the California credit: The federal version is uncapped. Despite its bipartisan support, some critics argue that the tax incentives would first and foremost benefit the richest players in the system - massive entities like Paramount Skydance and the star actors and directors who are their top moneymakers. “Do we really need kickbacks to corporations to employ a whole labor force?” asked Andi Brittan, a veteran set decorator and union leader at the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees Local 44. “Unfortunately, the truth is, we have to work within the system, and working within the system means supporting these kinds of tax incentives.” Other detractors point to past economic reports showing that these kinds of tax subsidies provide little to no quantifiable value. For example, a 2023 report published by the state of New York found that from 2012 to 2022, the tax incentives didn’t generate as many jobs as would have been created in other industries. Still, the report also noted there are probably indirect positive economic effects that are hard to quantify. That’s something many in the industry focus on. “It’s not just the films,” Mumm said. “It’s the trickling out - the florists, the food stylists, all of this stuff outside of the industry that rely on this huge force purchasing from them.” It may be too late to ever fully recover from years of being beat on production costs, and there’s still major concern about the impact of the Paramount Skydance acquisition of Warner Bros. Even so, the rank and file of the U.S. film industry are uttering words like “optimistic.” “I feel a good amount of hope, and I’ll tell you why,” said Kevin Armento, a film and TV writer. “All those soundstages are still sitting there. They haven’t bulldozed them yet.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/business/2026/10/17/tax-breaks-tinseltown-would-aim-keep-film-tv-production-us/
